reason: The sources provide rich, verified details across multiple independent sites about the 1862 discovery of Sirius B and its mind-bending physics.
story: Sirius is famous for being the brightest star in Earth's night sky, blazing just 8.6 light-years away in the constellation Canis Major. But in 1844, German astronomer Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel noticed a strange wobble in Sirius's path, deducing that an invisible companion was pulling on it. Eighteen years later, on January 31, 1862, American telescope maker Alvan Graham Clark spotted the hidden culprit while testing a giant 18.5-inch lens: a faint companion star now known as Sirius B. In 1915, astronomer Walter Adams analyzed its light and confirmed a mind-bending reality. Sirius B is a white dwarf star—the dead core of an ancient star that was once more massive than Sirius A. It packs roughly the entire mass of our Sun into a sphere smaller than planet Earth, making its material so dense that a single small sample weighs tons on Earth. Today, these two stars orbit each other every 50 years.
angle: Sirius B packs the entire mass of our Sun into a stellar core smaller than planet Earth, creating matter so dense that a single cubic inch weighs over a ton.

claims.claim: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky as seen from Earth.
Sirius is located in the constellation Canis Major, also known as the Greater Dog.
The Sirius star system lies approximately 8.6 light-years from Earth.
In 1844, German astronomer Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel deduced that Sirius had an unseen companion star from wobbles in its proper motion.
American telescope maker and astronomer Alvan Graham Clark first observed Sirius B on January 31, 1862.
Alvan Graham Clark discovered Sirius B while testing an 18.5-inch refractor telescope lens.
Sirius B is a white dwarf star.
In 1915, Walter Adams observed the spectrum of Sirius B at Mount Wilson Observatory to help confirm its identity as a compact white dwarf.
Sirius B packs approximately the entire mass of the Sun into a volume comparable to or smaller than Earth.
Sirius A has roughly twice the mass of the Sun.
Sirius A and Sirius B orbit each other in a binary cycle lasting approximately 50 years.
Sirius B was originally a more massive star than Sirius A before exhausting its nuclear fuel and shedding its outer layers.
Sirius B no longer generates heat through nuclear fusion and is slowly cooling over time.
Historical observations of Sirius's summer rising led to the phrase 'dog days of summer'.

disputed: Ancient color of Sirius: Classical scholars like Ptolemy and Seneca described Sirius as red, whereas contemporary Chinese sources recorded it as white. Modern astronomers attribute red reports to atmospheric reddening near the horizon; the script should attribute the red description as an ancient mystery or leave it out.

Exact weight per unit volume of Sirius B: Estimates in the sources range from 1 ton per cubic inch to 15 tons per cubic inch depending on calculated core vs average density. The script should stick to a general high-impact comparison like 'a single cubic inch weighs over a ton'.
